Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If oral contraceptives prevent ovulation, why don't they also extend a woman's fertility?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Let’s imagine a garden where flowers can grow seeds. In a woman’s body, there’s a special time every month when a tiny egg (like a seed) can be ready to grow into a baby if it meets a sperm.

Oral contraceptives (those are like special medicine pills) help stop the garden from getting ready to grow a seed every month—they kind of "tell" the garden to take a break and not get the egg ready.

But, if you stop taking those pills, the garden will start getting ready again, just like before. The pills don’t take away the ability to grow seeds forever—they just pause it while you’re taking them. That’s why they don’t make you less able to have a baby forever; they just stop you from getting pregnant while you’re using them.

So, the pills don’t make you less fertile (which means less able to have a baby), they just put things on pause!
